mindmapMd:
# Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT

## 1. Core Mental Model
- LLMs are stochastic token-autocomplete systems
- They predict one token at a time
- Useful, powerful, and unreliable in specific ways
- Use as tools; verify important outputs

## 2. Pre-training: Learning Internet Patterns
### Data collection
- Common Crawl and other web sources
- Huge, diverse document collections
- FineWeb example
  - 44 TB filtered text
  - About 15 trillion tokens
  - English-focused filtering

### Data cleaning
- URL and domain blocklists
- HTML-to-text extraction
- Language filtering
- Deduplication
- PII removal
- Quality and safety heuristics

### Tokenization
- Text becomes a one-dimensional sequence
- UTF-8 bits → bytes → tokens
- Byte Pair Encoding
  - Merge frequent symbol pairs
  - Shorter sequences, larger vocabulary
- GPT-4 tokenizer
  - Around 100,277 tokens
  - Spacing and capitalization matter
- Token IDs have no inherent meaning

### Next-token prediction
- Input: context window of prior tokens
- Output: probability for every vocabulary token
- Training adjusts parameters
  - Increase probability of correct next token
  - Decrease alternatives
- Loss measures prediction error
- Lower loss means better statistical modeling

### Transformers
- Parameterized mathematical functions
- Billions to trillions of weights
- Token embeddings
- Attention blocks
- MLP blocks
- Layer normalization and softmax
- Not biological brains
  - Fixed computation per token
  - No persistent memory inside one forward pass

### Inference
- Start with a prompt prefix
- Predict token probabilities
- Sample one token
- Append it to the context
- Repeat token by token
- Different samples can yield different continuations

## 3. Base Models
### What a base model is
- Result of pre-training
- Internet-document simulator
- Continues text rather than naturally assisting
- Generates web-like statistical continuations

### Scale and compute
- GPT-2
  - 1.6B parameters
  - 1,024-token context
  - About 100B training tokens
- Modern systems
  - Hundreds of billions or more parameters
  - Much larger datasets and contexts
- GPU clusters enable parallel training
- Training can cost tens or hundreds of millions

### Knowledge in weights
- Parameters act like lossy internet compression
- Common information is easier to recall
- Rare facts are vague and unreliable
- Some repeated training text can be memorized
  - Regurgitation risk
  - Near-verbatim continuations

### Knowledge cutoff
- Pre-training has a date boundary
- Later events are unavailable from weights
- Future-facing prompts invite probabilistic guesses
- Hallucinations can result

### In-context learning
- Examples in the prompt teach temporary patterns
- Few-shot prompting can induce tasks
  - Translation
  - Formatting
  - Classification
- The context window acts as working memory

## 4. Prompting Base Models
### Assistant prompting
- Frame text as a Human/Assistant conversation
- Include few-shot examples
- Add the actual user question last
- Base model continues the conversation pattern

### Limits
- Without a conversation format, prompts may continue oddly
- Base models may invent further turns
- Prompting alone is not robust assistant behavior

## 5. Post-training: Creating Assistants
### Goal
- Convert a base model into a helpful assistant
- Continue training on curated conversations
- Same next-token algorithm; different dataset

### Conversation datasets
- Human and assistant turns
- Multi-turn dialogue
- Helpful answers
- Friendly style
- Refusals for unsafe requests
- Hundreds of thousands to millions of examples

### Conversation encoding
- Special tokens mark:
  - Turn starts and ends
  - User role
  - Assistant role
  - System role
- Entire chat becomes one token sequence
- Generation begins after the assistant marker

### Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
- Human labelers write ideal responses
- Labeling guidance defines:
  - Helpfulness
  - Truthfulness
  - Harmlessness
  - Style and refusals
- Modern datasets often use:
  - LLM-generated drafts
  - Human edits
  - Synthetic conversations
  - Curated data mixtures

### Assistant persona
- Personality is learned from examples
- The model statistically imitates trained labelers
- A response resembles a simulation of:
  - A trained human labeler
  - Following company instructions
  - Drawing on pre-training knowledge

## 6. Hallucinations and Factuality
### Why hallucinations happen
- “Who is X?” training examples often receive confident answers
- Unknown names still trigger answer-shaped completions
- The model predicts plausible tokens, not truth
- It does not automatically research during inference

### Factuality training
- Identify facts the model knows versus does not know
- Ask factual questions repeatedly
- Compare answers with ground truth
- Train uncertainty-aware responses
  - “I don’t know”
  - “I don’t remember”
- Connect internal uncertainty to verbal refusal

### Tool use
- Give models structured tool-call tokens
- Example: web search
  - Generate search query
  - Pause generation
  - Retrieve results
  - Insert source text into context
  - Answer from fresh evidence
- Other tools
  - Code interpreter
  - Python execution
  - External APIs

### Parameters vs. context
- Parameters = vague long-term recollection
- Context window = direct working memory
- Better prompting
  - Paste source material
  - Attach documents
  - Provide relevant data
- Direct context is usually better than recalled knowledge

## 7. Model Identity and “Self”
### No persistent self
- A model processes a context and generates tokens
- It has no continuous personal existence
- Conversations are temporary token contexts
- Identity claims can be hallucinated

### Identity controls
- Fine-tuning examples can teach a name and origin
- Hidden system messages can specify:
  - Model name
  - Developer
  - Knowledge cutoff
  - Behavioral instructions
- Self-description is supplied through data and context

## 8. Cognitive Sharp Edges
### Models need tokens to think
- Each token gets limited computation
- Immediate answers force large reasoning leaps
- Intermediate steps distribute computation
- Good solution traces expose useful subproblems

### Arithmetic failures
- One-token or rushed answers can be wrong
- Longer step-by-step reasoning can help
- Code tools are better for exact calculations

### Counting and spelling failures
- Models see tokens, not individual characters
- A word may span several tokens
- Counting dots or letters can fail
- Character indexing is better delegated to code

### Strange capability gaps
- Models may solve difficult problems yet fail simple ones
- Token associations can interfere with reasoning
- Example class: decimal comparisons
- Capabilities resemble Swiss cheese
  - Broad competence
  - Unexpected holes

## 9. Reinforcement Learning (RL)
### Why SFT is insufficient
- Human-written solutions may not be optimal for models
- Human reasoning differs from model reasoning
- Some solution traces are:
  - Too abrupt
  - Too verbose
  - Too difficult
  - Mismatched with model knowledge

### RL as guess-and-check
- Provide prompts and verifiable answers
- Sample many candidate solutions
- Score successful versus unsuccessful attempts
- Reinforce paths that reach correct answers
- Model-generated traces become training material

### SFT and RL roles
- SFT
  - Initializes expert-like behavior
  - Teaches solution formats
- RL
  - Optimizes methods that work for the model
  - Encourages reliable answer paths
  - Refines reasoning through trial and error

### Reasoning emergence
- RL models often generate longer traces
- They may:
  - Recheck calculations
  - Backtrack
  - Reframe problems
  - Try alternatives
  - Verify final answers
- Chains of thought can emerge from optimization
- More tokens can improve difficult-problem accuracy

### Thinking models
- Useful for hard math and coding
- Slower than ordinary assistant models
- Visible answers may summarize hidden reasoning
- Best used selectively for demanding tasks

## 10. RL and AlphaGo
### AlphaGo lesson
- Supervised imitation plateaued near human expert play
- Self-play RL optimized winning directly
- RL discovered strategies humans did not expect
- Move 37 illustrated non-human but effective play

### LLM potential
- RL may discover new reasoning strategies
- Possible future capabilities
  - Novel analogies
  - Unusual problem decompositions
  - Non-human solution paths
- Requires large, diverse practice environments

## 11. Verifiable vs. Unverifiable RL
### Verifiable domains
- Math
- Code
- Games
- Concrete answer checking
- Scoring is difficult to game
- Can support long-running optimization

### Unverifiable domains
- Jokes
- Poems
- Creative writing
- Summaries
- Quality is subjective and expensive to assess

### RLHF
- Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
- Humans rank candidate outputs
- Train a reward model to predict preferences
- Run RL against the reward-model simulator

### RLHF strengths
- Scales preference learning
- Works for subjective domains
- Ranking is easier than writing ideal answers
- Can improve helpfulness and style

### RLHF limits
- Reward models are imperfect human simulators
- RL can exploit reward-model weaknesses
- Adversarial outputs can score highly
- Long optimization may collapse into nonsense
- Usually requires early stopping and careful monitoring

## 12. Future Directions
### Multimodality
- Text, images, audio, and video become token streams
- Models can:
  - Hear and speak
  - See and generate images
  - Combine modalities in one context
- Same broad training logic applies

### Agents
- Models increasingly take actions over time
- Potential tasks:
  - Browser use
  - Keyboard and mouse control
  - Multi-step workflows
  - Progress reporting
- Humans will increasingly supervise agents
- Reliability and monitoring remain essential

### Test-time learning
- Current deployed weights are fixed
- Only context changes during inference
- In-context learning is limited and temporary
- Long-running tasks need better memory and learning methods
- Larger context windows alone may not scale indefinitely

## 13. Using and Tracking Models
### Model sources
- Proprietary providers
  - ChatGPT
  - Gemini
  - Other major labs
- Open-weight hosting
  - Inference providers such as Together AI
- Base-model hosting
  - Providers such as Hyperbolic
- Local models
  - Smaller or distilled models
  - Lower-precision variants
  - Tools such as LM Studio

### Tracking progress
- Human-preference leaderboards
- AI newsletters
- Research papers and technical releases
- Trusted researchers and practitioners on social platforms
- Test models on real personal tasks

## 14. What Happens When You Send a Chat Message?
### Request pipeline
- Your text is tokenized
- It is placed into a conversation protocol
- System, user, and prior assistant turns form one sequence
- The model predicts and samples the next tokens
- Those tokens become the response

### Where the response comes from
- Pre-training
  - Internet knowledge compressed into parameters
- SFT
  - Assistant behavior and personality
  - Statistical imitation of trained labelers
- RL for thinking models
  - Optimized reasoning paths
  - Trial-and-error problem-solving strategies

## 15. Closing Guidance
- LLMs dramatically accelerate work
- Use them for:
  - Brainstorming
  - First drafts
  - Explanations
  - Coding assistance
  - Research support
- Do not trust outputs blindly
- Check facts, math, and citations
- Prefer fresh context and tools for accuracy
- Remain responsible for the final work
summaryMd:
Large language models are token-based neural networks trained to predict and generate text. ChatGPT-like assistants emerge through pre-training, post-training, tool use, and—in some models—reinforcement learning.

- **Pre-training compresses internet text into model weights:** Curated web data is filtered, deduplicated, stripped of PII, tokenized, and used to teach next-token prediction.
- **Tokens are text chunks, not words or characters:** Byte-pair encoding builds a large vocabulary that shortens sequences, but makes character-level tasks unreliable.
- **Transformers predict one token at a time:** Given a context window, the network outputs probabilities for every possible next token and samples one repeatedly.
- **Training and inference are distinct:** Training adjusts fixed parameters over huge datasets; deployed chat interaction usually performs inference without changing those weights.
- **A base model is sophisticated autocomplete:** It simulates internet-document patterns and can contain broad knowledge, but is not inherently an assistant.
- **Base-model knowledge is probabilistic and lossy:** Frequent patterns may be recalled well, rare facts may be wrong, and some training text can be memorized or regurgitated.
- **Prompting can temporarily shape behavior:** Few-shot examples and conversation framing can make a base model continue as if it were an assistant.
- **Post-training creates the assistant persona:** Continued training on curated human–assistant conversations teaches helpfulness, refusals, style, and task-following.
- **Assistant responses imitate curated examples:** A useful model is roughly a statistical simulation of how trained labelers would respond under company instructions.
- **Conversation protocols are token sequences:** Special tokens mark system, user, and assistant turns so the model can generate the next assistant response.
- **Hallucinations arise from answer-shaped prediction:** When uncertain, a model may produce a confident, plausible continuation instead of admitting it lacks a fact.
- **Factuality training can teach abstention:** Models can be trained to say they do not know when evaluations show their stored knowledge is unreliable.
- **Tools extend the model’s working memory:** Search, code execution, and other tool outputs can be inserted into the context window, improving factuality and computation.
- **Context beats vague recollection:** Supplying source text directly usually yields better summaries or analysis than asking the model to rely only on parameters.
- **Model identity is not intrinsic self-knowledge:** Claims about a model’s name, creator, or cutoff are generally supplied through fine-tuning data or system messages.
- **Models need tokens to think:** Because each token has limited computation, intermediate reasoning steps often improve performance over forced immediate answers.
- **Use code for exact computation:** Mental arithmetic, counting, spelling, and character manipulation can fail because models operate over tokens rather than characters.
- **Capabilities are “Swiss cheese”:** Models can solve difficult problems yet fail unexpectedly on simple tasks, so outputs require verification.
- **Reinforcement learning improves verifiable reasoning:** Models generate many candidate solutions, receive rewards for correct outcomes, and reinforce successful reasoning paths.
- **Thinking models use longer solution traces:** RL can produce checking, backtracking, alternate approaches, and more reliable performance on domains such as math and code.
- **RLHF extends optimization to subjective tasks:** Human rankings train reward models that scale preference feedback, but optimization can eventually exploit reward-model flaws.
- **RL may discover nonhuman strategies:** Like AlphaGo’s unexpected Move 37, large-scale RL could uncover useful reasoning approaches outside human solution patterns.
- **Multimodality uses the same broad recipe:** Audio and image representations can be tokenized and combined with text in a shared context window.
- **Agents are a developing direction:** Models may increasingly execute multi-step tasks over time, but still need supervision, monitoring, and error correction.
- **Current models do not truly learn at test time:** Their parameters remain fixed during deployment; only the finite context window changes.
- **Practical guidance is to treat LLMs as tools:** Use them for drafting, exploration, and acceleration, but check sources, verify calculations, and remain responsible for results.
slidesHtml:
A visual field guide

Deep Dive into
LLMs like ChatGPT

From internet text to token-by-token conversation—and the sharp edges that matter in practice.

01

Pre-training

The internet becomes a training corpus.

2.7Bweb pages indexed by Common Crawl as of 2024
44 TBFineWeb after aggressive text filtering
15Tapproximate tokens in that filtered corpus
Filter URLs, extract text, identify language, remove PII, deduplicate.02

Representation

Text is compressed into tokens.

Raw textA one-dimensional stream of characters.
Bytes8 bits make one of 256 symbols.
Byte pair encodingFrequent chunks become new symbols.
TokensSmall text chunks with arbitrary IDs.

GPT-4 uses a vocabulary of 100,277 tokens. “hello world” becomes two.

03

The core machine

A Transformer predicts
the next token.

INPUTContext tokens enter a parameterized mathematical function.

OUTPUTA probability distribution across the entire vocabulary.

TRAINRaise probability on the known next token; repeat at massive scale.

GENERATESample one token, append it, then predict again.

Weights are fixed during a normal ChatGPT conversation.04

Base model → assistant

Post-training changes the behavior—not the basic algorithm.

Base modelAn internet-document simulator: stochastic autocomplete, not yet an assistant.
Supervised fine-tuningTrain on curated human/assistant conversations with special turn tokens.
KnowledgeStored vaguely and statistically in billions of learned parameters.
PersonaLearned by example from labeler instructions and ideal responses.
Useful mental model: a response imitates what a skilled labeler would write.05

Sharp edge / factuality

A fluent answer is not proof of knowledge. It may be a statistically plausible fabrication.

Hallucination

“Who is X?” training patterns can trigger a confident invented biography for an unknown name.

Calibrated refusal

Post-training can teach the model to say “I don’t know” when internal uncertainty is high.

Tools

Search inserts fresh source text into the context window, enabling grounded answers and citations.

Parameters = vague recollection. Context window = working memory.06

Sharp edge / computation

Models need tokens
to think.

01Each next-token prediction has finite compute.

02Intermediate steps place useful results back into the context window.

03Direct one-token answers encourage premature guesses.

04For arithmetic, counting, spelling, and code: ask for a tool.

The model sees token chunks—not necessarily individual letters, dots, or digits.

07

Third stage

Reinforcement learning:
guess, check, reinforce.

PromptA problem with a verifiable final answer.
Many rolloutsSample thousands or millions of possible solution paths.
ScoreKeep paths that reach the correct result.
UpdateMake successful patterns more likely next time.
RL can discover longer reasoning traces, checks, retries, and strategies that work for the model.08

Reasoning & alignment

Not all feedback scales equally.

Verifiable RLMath, code, and games: clear outcomes can support long optimization runs.
Thinking modelsUse extra tokens to explore, backtrack, check, then present a concise answer.
RLHFA reward model learns to approximate human preference from ranked outputs.
Reward hackingOptimize too long and the model can exploit the reward model with nonsense.
RLHF helps—but it is not an indefinitely scalable substitute for objective verification.09

What comes next

More modalities.
Longer-running agents.
New memory ideas.

Multimodality

Text, audio, and image tokens can share one context window.

Agents

Models increasingly operate tools over seconds, minutes, or hours—with supervision.

Test-time learning

Today’s deployed weights stay fixed; context is finite working memory, not durable learning.

The core challenge: coherent, error-correcting work over long multimodal tasks.10

Closing

Use LLMs as powerful tools—not unquestioned authorities.

CHECKHallucinations and “Swiss cheese” failures remain.

GROUNDPut source material in context; use search and code when appropriate.

OWNYou remain responsible for the final work.

Token autocomplete can be astonishingly capable. Careful use makes it genuinely useful.
